items.stem: Users ask about 'time off' but the docs say 'leave', and retrieval misses the answer. The most direct fix is:

options.text: Rewrite or expand the query to bridge the vocabulary gap
options.rationale: Correct: query rewriting aligns user wording with document terminology to improve recall.
Document length is not the mismatch cause.

options.text: Use a bigger model to guess
options.rationale: The passage was never retrieved; generation cannot fix a retrieval miss.

items.explanation: Correct: query rewriting aligns user wording with document terminology to improve recall.

items.stem: Which TWO describe good retrieval routing? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Directing product-specific questions to that product's index
options.rationale: Correct: routing to the relevant source improves precision and recall.

options.text: Defining a fallback when no route is confident
options.rationale: Correct: a fallback prevents dropped queries when routing is uncertain.

options.text: Sending every query to one index regardless of topic
options.rationale: Ignoring topic defeats the purpose of routing.

options.text: Routing by the length of the question only
options.rationale: Length is not a meaningful routing signal.

items.explanation: Correct: routing to the relevant source improves precision and recall.

items.stem: A query rewrite boosted one demo question but you suspect regressions. The honest next step is:

options.text: Evaluate the rewrite across a labelled set to check average impact
options.rationale: Correct: measuring across many queries reveals whether the average improved.

options.text: Ship it because the demo looked good
options.rationale: A single demo can hide regressions.
That removes the capability rather than evaluating the change.
Rewrites can help some queries and hurt others.
